supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Weather Local NBC NY 24/7 Video Newsletters Investigations Baquero Our Voices Watch 24/7 Create profile / Log in Dashboard Email preferences Sign out Trending Streaming News 24/7 New York Live Celebrity News Trump Administration Immigration NY Giants War With Iran Send Photos/Videos Open House Expand Health How bad will this flu season be? What to expect after ‘superflu' winter As respiratory virus season approaches, experts discuss what we may expect this flu season and how to protect yourself. By Caroline Kee | TODAY • Published September 9, 2026 • Updated on September 9, 2026 at 1:58 pm BOOKMARKER Summer isn’t officially over yet, but respiratory viruses are already beginning to ramp up across the United States. Seasonal influenza activity is still low compared to COVID-19, but experts are already urging people to prepare for flu season. Last winter, the country faced an unprecedented, severe flu epidemic fueled by the highly mutated H3N2 subclade K flu variant, dubbed the “super flu.” Watch NBC 4 free wherever you are WATCH HERE It was one of the worst flu seasons in decades, and doctors’ visits for flu-like illness reached the highest levels seen in over 25 years, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Earlier this year, scientists updated the 2026-2027 flu shots to protect against the subclade K strain. As vaccines are rolled out, you may be wondering what to expect in the coming months. In the U.S., flu activity typically peaks between December and February, per the CDC. But the timing and severity of flu seasons can vary from year to year. Are there any signs that the flu virus could mutate again this fall? Could we be in for another severe flu season, and how can you protect yourself? TODAY.com spoke to experts to find out. How bad will the 2026-2027 flu season be? “The only thing that’s predictable about influenza is it’s unpredictable,” Dr. Daniel Jernigan, a former CDC director and a contributing scholar at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. It’s still too early to tell how the 2026-2027 flu season will unfold, but there are some early clues, experts say. Predicting the severity of flu seasons is a delicate art, Dr. Albert Ko, professor of epidemiology at Yale School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. Scientists use a combination of forecasting models and look at trends in the Southern hemisphere, which experiences its winter and flu season earlier in the year. Australia is often viewed as a harbinger for what to expect stateside. Australia’s 2026 flu season has been moderate so far, and much milder compared to last season — the country’s busiest and deadliest in decades, says Ko. Data shows cases are surging later than usual, but are nowhere near the peak in 2025. “I wouldn’t sound the warning signs about what’s happening in Australia now,” says Ko. However, flu activity in the Southern hemisphere isn’t always a reliable indicator, and sometimes the U.S. trends don’t follow. “It’s not linear,” Jernigan adds. It’s also rare to see two severe flu seasons back-to-back, but that’s exactly what happened last winter. The 2024-2025 flu season was considered “high severity,” per the CDC, and it was followed by another record-breaking season last winter. “I did not expect the big season last year because we just had a bad season. ... It flummoxed most of us who follow flu closely,” Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist and professor of medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells TODAY.com. While there are some early signs to suggest we’re in for a milder flu season, “always prepare for the worst,” Schaffner says. Cold and flu season is on the way, and some of the leading U.S. medical groups are offering their own guidance on vaccinations. Is there a new flu variant? So far, there is no evidence that a new, mutated flu variant will drive cases this flu season, the experts say. There are two main types of influenza that cause seasonal epidemics: influenza A (H3N2 and H1N1) and influenza B. Last winter’s flu surge, as well as the Southern hemisphere’s 2026 flu season, was fueled largely by H3N2 subclade K. The highly contagious variant emerged early last year, and has seven mutations that caused it to “drift” from the H3N2 strain in the flu shot. “We’re always worried about antigenic shifts, or changes in those viruses because that can set off larger and expected seasonal waves of of influenza,” says Ko. So far, there’s no evidence that the flu virus has picked up significant mutations that set it apart from the strains circulating, including H3N2 subclade K, according to the experts. But experts remain cautious because the influenza virus mutates constantly. “The virus is in control ... and until you actually go through it, you’re never 100% certain,” Dr. Ronald Nahass, president of the Infectious Disease Society of America, tells TODAY.com. A significant portion of the U.S. population still has not been exposed to subclade K and may be at risk, Jernigan notes, adding “we’re (still) closely watching subclade K.” Flu symptoms The flu isn’t a mild cold. The symptoms are intense and start suddenly — what many experts describe as feeling like “being hit by a truck.” The most common signs of flu infection include: Severe fatigue Fever Chills Body aches Runny or stuffy nose Sore throat Cough Less commonly, the flu may cause diarrhea and vomiting, which is more common among children than adults, per the CDC. Most healthy people will recover from flu on their own, but it can cause you to feel miserable for up to two weeks. Adults over the age of 65, children under 5, pregnant women and immunocompromised people are at higher risk for severe disease or complications from the flu, says Schaffner. However, the flu can become deadly for anyone. If you develop severe flu symptoms or you’re in a high-risk group, contact your healthcare provider, says Schaffner. It’s cold and flu season again, which means you could be left wondering which virus is causing your symptoms. Here’s what you need to know. Flu tests and treatments The only way to know if you have the flu is to get tested. The experts recommend stocking up on 3-in-1 rapid home tests for influenza A, influenza B and COVID-19 ahead of the fall. If you test positive, there are treatment options available. Antiviral drugs help the body fight the flu virus, which can help lessen symptoms and shorten the duration of illness by a day or two, per the CDC. Flu treatment is most important for people who develop severe symptoms or are in a high-risk group, the experts note. Flu antivirals require a positive flu test and a prescription from a doctor, and work best when started within one to two days after you start feeling sick, the experts note. Are the new flu shots available? Vaccination is the most effective way to protect yourself from the flu, the experts emphasize. The influenza vaccine reduces the risk of severe disease, complications and death. It’s not 100% effective. “You can get flu vaccine and still get the flu. That does not mean that the vaccine has failed. It’s designed to keep you out of the hospital, out of the intensive care unit, and out of the cemetery,” Schaffner adds. The 2026-2027 flu vaccines are available and being rolled out at pharmacies, doctor’s offices and hospitals across the country. The shots are trivalent, per the CDC, which means they protect against three viruses: influenza A H1N1 (pdm09), influenza A H3N2, and influenza B (Victoria lineage). There are multiple vaccine options available this year. These include standard egg-based flu shots, high-dose shots, cell-based shots and a nasal mist. Last month, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a new mRNA flu vaccine from Moderna for adults ages 50 and older. The mRNA flu vaccine was shown to be about 27% more effective than standard flu shots in a trial, NBC News reported. These are safe, and the mRNA technology is very promising, Nahass notes. Although the mRNA shots are expected to be available this fall, supply will likely be limited, Schaffner notes. “I encourage people to talk to their physicians about which vaccine they should get. There are lots of choices,” says Nahass. 2026-2027 flu shot guidelines The CDC usually makes an official federal recommendation for flu vaccines every September. This guides providers, patients, and insurers. However, the expert panel in charge of this decision, the Advisory Committee for Immunization Practices (ACIP), was sidelined earlier this year. Instead, the CDC stated that its guidance from 2025 would remain in effect for the 2026-2027 season — which creates confusion, experts say. In lieu of new guidelines, leading medical groups came together with the Vaccine Integrity Project to issue a joint vaccine recommendation ahead of respiratory virus season. These include the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Medicine, American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the Infectious Disease Society of America. “It’s our collaborative effort to fill the void by the CDC and the ACIP, which didn’t provide up-to-date guidance regarding respiratory vaccines,” says Nahass. The groups strongly recommended that everyone ages 6 months and older (including pregnant women) get an annual flu vaccine, and people who are ages 65 or older or have weakened immune systems get a high-dose flu shot. These guidelines were based on evidence published in JAMA showing the flu vaccine protects against severe disease and cuts the risk of hospitalization, especially for high-risk groups. “Since the risks of the vaccine are so low and the benefits are so great, the medical community has come down strongly to recommend that folks get vaccinated,” says Nahass. If you have questions, talk to your doctor. When is the best time to get a flu shot? The best time to get a flu shot is late September or October, experts say. “We want the protection to extend throughout the winter, beyond February into March. That’s a pretty long reach, and so you don’t want to get the flu vaccine too early,” says Schaffner. It takes about two weeks for the body to respond and the flu shot to take full effect, and this protection lasts around six months. While it’s never “too late” to get a flu shot, the experts encourage people not to wait until flu activity is spiking. “It’s not as useful once we’re in the wave. You’re going to get most bang for the buck by getting the flu shot earlier,” says Ko. Similarly, the experts urge parents to vaccinate their children before the flu is sweeping through schools. “There are children who die each year of influenza. It’s a great tragedy. The vast majority of them are unvaccinated, but about half of the children who die are healthy,” says Schaffner. How to protect against flu If you’re concerned about the flu, your best bet is getting the flu shot. Vaccination is the most effective way to protect yourself, but you can take extra tried-and-true actions to fight the spread of respiratory viruses, Schaffner notes. Here are some more tips going into flu season: Wear a well-fitted N95 or mask in crowded settings. Wash your hands frequently. Test if you have symptoms. Contact your healthcare provider if you get sick. Cover coughs and sneezes. Avoid contact with sick people. “Listen to your doctors,” says Nahass. This story first appeared on TODAY.com. supplementary_news.content_title: Flu Cases Surge in Shanghai and Hangzhou as Schools Report Classwide Isolation
supplementary_news.content: Multiple classes across Shanghai are sent home for isolation, with some classes shut down entirely. One Shanghai parent posts on social media asking: "What's going on with the flu in Shanghai?" (Screenshot via NTD) Flu cases are climbing sharply across Shanghai and Hangzhou just as the new school semester gets underway, prompting a wave of classwide quarantines and school closures across the two cities' primary schools and kindergartens. The Chinese regime’s state-run and local government-affiliated outlets—including Hangzhou News and Nanjing Morning Post—along with individual Weibo users, have published multiple accounts describing crowded pediatric wards, sudden school notices, and families scrambling to keep up as the outbreak spreads through classrooms in both cities. The disruption has hit families within days of the semester starting. In Hangzhou, the capital city of China's east coastal Zhejiang Province, one mother said her third-grade daughter's teacher sent a text just a week into the term. “10 of the roughly 40 students in the class had already gone home with fevers, and about half tested positive for flu,” Li said, cited by Hangzhou News Center. Her daughter is a year-3 primary pupil who was not affected by the flu. Li said that, under local health authority requirements, the entire class was ordered to quarantine at home for four days, from Sept. 11 to Sept. 14, before returning to school Sept. 15. Parents describe similar scenes playing out across Shanghai, one of China's major financial hubs roughly 120 miles northeast of Hangzhou. One parent wrote on social media: "What's going on with the flu in Shanghai? We got a notice first thing in the morning that the whole class was quarantined, and by afternoon we found out half the kids were out sick," according to a report by Nanjing Morning Post on Sept. 14. The publication in Nanjing reported another case of quarantine in Shanghai: one flu case, a four-day shutdown for the whole class. According to the publication, at 4:41 p.m. on Sept. 2, a parent in Baoshan, a northern suburb of Shanghai, received a notice in a group chat from the head teacher: "We’ve had one case of seasonal flu confirmed in the class. Per requirements from the local health authority, Class Da Yi (equivalent to Pre-K in the U.S. system) will undergo a four-day quarantine period, from Sept. 2 to Sept. 5. Kids can come back to class as normal on Sept. 7." A blogger by the name Tingxintang also posted this case on China’s digital mouthpiece NetEase, adding that, with less than two weeks into the new semester, multiple classes across Shanghai had been sent home for isolation one after another, with some schools shutting down entirely. China's National Disease Control and Prevention Administration (NDCPA) addressed the outbreak of the flu, claiming that the strains currently circulating nationally are influenza A (subtypes H1N1 and H3N2) and influenza B (Victoria lineage), which tend to circulate in alternation or overlap to produce each year's seasonal wave. A Third of Hospital Beds Now Occupied by Kids Infected with Flu: Doctor Dr. Qi Zhenghong, chief physician of the infectious disease department at Hangzhou Children's Hospital, said flu-related outpatient visits and hospital admissions among children have risen sharply since the semester began, according to Hangzhou News Center. "Before this, we just had a handful of flu patients in the ward here and there," Qi said. "Now flu cases make up about a third of our hospital beds, with roughly 10 kids admitted every single day." Qi said this season's dominant strain is influenza A H3N2, mixed in with influenza B's Victoria strain, and that kids in kindergarten and the early grades of elementary school are getting hit the hardest. She's also seeing a clear pattern: once one person in a household gets sick, the whole family tends to go down one by one. In one case, a grandmother came down with the flu first and passed it to her 3-year-old grandson, who ran a high fever for days and had it worse than the adults did. Not long after, both parents got sick too. Qi said many household outbreaks followed the same pattern: an adult picked up the virus outside, brought it home, and passed it to a kid with a weaker immune system, who later spread it to the whole family. "Kids also tend to stay sick longer than adults do, which makes it that much easier for the flu to spread through an entire household," Qi said. The NDCPA said China's flu season typically runs from autumn through winter and early spring, entering its high-transmission period between November and March, with the seasonal peak usually landing in mid-to-late December through early January. Northern provinces see a clear winter-spring peak, while southern provinces—in addition to that same winter-spring peak—sometimes also experience a secondary summer wave of flu activity. The blogger Tingxintang shared a Shanghai parent's question: "Is the flu hitting Shanghai earlier than usual this year?" Conversation Conversations are moderated. Aberdeen, Scotland, September 14, 2026 -- Following a record-breaking year where experienced pharmacists administered over 1,000 vaccines during the previous winter, Bucksburn Pharmacy & Health Clinic has officially announced the continuation of its comprehensive private vaccination program. The clinic will continue providing the flu jab in Aberdeen to patients for the upcoming 2026/2027 season, ensuring local residents and businesses maintain vital protection against seasonal influenza. With NHS eligibility criteria tightening in recent years, primarily reserving free vaccines for adults aged 65 and over or those with specific high-risk health conditions, millions of individuals across the region find themselves without access to free protection. Bucksburn Pharmacy & Health Clinic fills this critical healthcare gap by delivering convenient, self-funded private vaccinations to anyone aged six months and above who falls outside the public funding guidelines. Patients visiting the trusted local pharmacy receive direct, face-to-face consultations with skilled clinical staff to verify suitability before receiving their injection. To accommodate varying patient needs and clinical profiles, the health clinic stocks a diverse selection of advanced vaccines from major manufacturers, including cell-based, sub-unit, and nasal spray options such as QiVe trivalent from Sanofi and Flucelvax from Seqirus. To make winter health precautions as seamless as possible, the clinic offers an intuitive online booking system. Patients can select preferred appointment slots, pay a booking deposit, receive instant email confirmations, and settle remaining fees upon arrival. Standard individual appointments are priced at £30, with specialized corporate discounts available for local companies booking groups of 10 or more employees. Located on Inverurie Road, the independent health center offers far more than traditional prescription fulfillment. In addition to seasonal influenza protection, the clinic acts as a full-spectrum community health hub, delivering dedicated travel vaccination clinics, specialized skin treatments via cryotherapy, and advanced ear care, including microsuction wax removal. The independent facility also continues to offer free prescription collection and delivery services throughout Aberdeen. Appointments for the current rollout begin in late September and run continuously through the winter months. Members of the public, families, and business owners looking to secure protection for the season can book directly through the clinic's website or contact the health team via phone or email for custom group arrangements. About Bucksburn Pharmacy & Health Clinic Formerly a Lloyds branch, Bucksburn Pharmacy & Health Clinic is an independent community pharmacy located in Aberdeen, Scotland. Driven by clinical excellence and patient safety, its team of experienced healthcare professionals provides essential primary care services, prescription management, and specialized clinic treatments to the local population. supplementary_news.content: 流感疫苗四价转三价,政策红利能否打开市场空间? 21新健康韩利明 2026-09-10 19:40 允许职工医保个人账户支付在定点医疗机构发生的流感疫苗费用 21世纪经济报道记者 韩利明 每年9月至次年5月,是我国流感病毒流行的高发期。时值金秋开学季,流感疫苗接种进入关键窗口期。 日前,在国家疾控局举行的新闻发布会上,中日友好医院呼吸与危重症医学科主任医师曹彬指出,每一个流感季,常见的流行毒株是有差异的,目前流行的主要是两种甲型流感和一种乙型流感,甲型流感是H1N1(简称甲1)、H3N2(简称甲3),乙型流感现在比较流行的是Victoria系的流感病毒。 “不同的流感流行季,推荐流感疫苗的组分也是不一样的,流感疫苗株是世界卫生组织根据全球流感监测的主要流行亚型来推荐的。因此,每年推荐的流感疫苗株也是有所差别的。所以说,需要大家能够充分理解,并每年适时接种今年适用的流感疫苗。”曹彬强调。 结合中国疾病预防控制中心9月2日发布的《中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南(2026—2027)》(下称《指南》),2026年流感疫苗最大的变化是“四价转三价”。这并非疫苗“减配”,而是基于病毒流行趋势的科学调整。 本次调整系因世界卫生组织监测发现,乙型Yamagata系毒株自2020年3月后已无主流传播风险,2026年—2027年流感季全球统一推荐使用三价流感疫苗,不再纳入该毒株组分。更新后的三价疫苗精准覆盖WHO预判的当前流行的甲型H1N1、H3N2和乙型Victoria系毒株。 建议在9—10月完成接种 国家流感中心最新监测数据显示,截至2026年8月30日当周,南方省份流感病毒检测阳性率上升、北方省份流感活动水平低,全国A(H3N2)占比升高。全国未报告流感样病例暴发疫情。 不过《指南》提醒,通常接种流感疫苗2—4周后,可产生具有保护水平的抗体。综合我国南、北方的流感流行特点,通常在11月份左右进入冬春季流感流行季,建议在9—10月完成接种;即使此时间段内未完成接种,整个流行季也都可以接种。 《指南》建议所有6月龄及以上且无接种禁忌的人接种流感疫苗,且优先推荐以下重点和高风险人群接种,包括医务人员、60岁及以上的老年人、罹患一种或多种慢性病者、养老机构及福利院等人群聚集场所脆弱人群及员工、6月龄—5岁儿童、托幼机构及中小学校等重点场所人群等。 疫苗品类方面,《指南》推荐三价流感疫苗,包括三价灭活疫苗(IIV3)和三价减毒活疫苗(LAIV3)。其中IIV3有裂解疫苗和亚单位疫苗,可用于6月龄及以上人群;LAIV3适用于3—17岁人群。 21世纪经济报道记者注意到,近期多地医院及社区卫生服务中心开放疫苗接种预约,价格各异。例如永胜县中医医院引入3款流感疫苗,疫苗价格分别为63元/剂、98元/剂、308元/剂,另收取15元/剂接种服务费。 根据相关报道,成都市成华区青龙社区卫生服务中心最近一周流感疫苗接种量约600至700人次;三价裂解灭活疫苗(6月龄及以上适用)75元/剂,已包含接种服务费;3—17岁适用鼻喷三价减毒活疫苗328元/剂(含服务费)。 南京市玄武门社区卫生服务中心公示信息显示,华兰流感裂解疫苗6—35月龄儿童接种2剂,价格为68元/剂;3岁及以上人群单剂接种,单价88元/剂。江苏中慧元通流感亚单位疫苗6—35月龄人群接种2剂;3岁及以上人群单剂,疫苗价格298元/剂。 批签发节奏分化,政策红利有望打开增长空间 从疫苗产业供给端看,西南证券研报此前有数据显示,流感疫苗主要包括三价流感疫苗、亚单位疫苗、四价流感疫苗和冻干鼻喷流感疫苗。2026年上半年流感疫苗批签发9批次,同比下滑93%。其中,三价流感疫苗批签发5批次;亚单位疫苗和四价流感疫苗获批签发均为2批次。 其中,三价流感疫苗获批签发5批次,同比下滑89%,全部来自于科兴生物;亚单位流感疫苗获批签发2批次,同比下滑50%,全部来自于中慧元通;四价流感疫苗批签发2批次,同比下滑97%,全部来自于科兴生物;鼻喷流感疫苗上半年未获批签发,从竞争格局看,鼻喷流感疫苗全部来自百克生物。 21世纪经济报道记者初步统计,今年6月底至今,国内流感疫苗累计批签发49批次。市场观察人士指出,经历前几年价格战后,国内流感疫苗市场份额持续向头部企业集中。 回溯2024年,国内流感疫苗龙头华兰疫苗下调四价流感疫苗产品价格,核心产品降价幅度约30%。2025年其流感疫苗业务营收11.21亿元,同比增长4.43%,业务呈现回暖,但受价格战余波影响,板块毛利率同比下降2.77%。 2026年上半年,受行业整体批签发周期节奏影响,华兰疫苗暂无流感疫苗新批次完成批签发与销售,相关板块营收同比下滑。不过截至2026年8月,该公司共取得流感疫苗批签发16批次。 鼻喷赛道方面,百克生物感雾®是国内首款鼻腔喷雾给药的流感减毒活疫苗,其液体剂型鼻喷流感疫苗于7月获得批签发、8月初启动上市销售,丰富了国内儿童青少年的接种选择。 整体来看,目前我国流感疫苗总体接种率约3%,远低于欧美接近50%的接种率。同时,WHO提出老人、小孩、慢病患者等重点人群流感疫苗接种率要达到75%的目标,目前国内重点人群覆盖率还不足5%。业内预期,随着政策积极推动、公众接种意识提升,接种率将不断提升,流感疫苗市场增长空间广阔。 政策层面利好持续释放。2026年5月,国家医保局办公室首次明确,允许职工医保个人账户支付在定点医疗机构发生的流感疫苗费用;2026年7月,国务院印发《国民健康“十五五”规划》,提出推动二级及以上医疗机构提供预防接种服务,推行疫苗处方政策。 有业内人士向21世纪经济报道记者表示,长远来看,疫苗行业属于品种为王、技术驱动的赛道,伴随流感疫苗技术迭代、鼻喷等新型疫苗普及,以及全民防疫认知提升、配套接种政策落地,具备技术创新能力、完善的产品矩阵和渠道覆盖优势的头部企业,将持续抢占市场份额,引领行业高质量扩容。 (作者:韩利明 编辑:季媛媛,张明艳) supplementary_news.content_title: Why This Year’s Flu Vaccine Is a Game-Changer for Kids
supplementary_news.content: Fort Worth, September 10 , 2026 | 09:01 AM America/Chicago Off the Sidelines: Why This Year’s Flu Vaccine Is a Game-Changer for Kids Marc Mazade, M.D. Written by Marc Mazade, M.D., MPH, m edical director of Infection Control and Prevention at Cook Children's My high school basketball coach insisted that we get a flu vaccine every year. He knew that flu is much more than just a cold. Flu is like getting hit by a train. He knew that recovery could take a couple of weeks. Flu vaccines might make you feel bad for a day, but feeling bad is a sign that our immune systems are working. That’s much better than getting knocked out of the game, missing a week of band competition, missing the big trip, or staying in bed while others exchange holiday gifts and treats. Flu season can run from November to May, so getting the flu vaccine in fall provides the longest protection from flu. During the last flu season, nearly 6,000 kids came to the emergency department and nearly 600 kids were hospitalized with flu at Cook Children’s Medical Center in Fort Worth (some would say an average season). Keeping folks out of the hospital is the main benefit of getting a flu vaccine, but not the only one. Because flu is passed between friends at school then spreads to family members, immunizing kids is key to controlling flu outbreaks. Closing hard-hit schools worsens hospital staff shortages as working parents must take off work to be with their kids, even when their kids aren’t sick. That can mean longer waiting times for patients and more shifts for exhausted health care workers. In 2025, the seasonal flu story got more interesting. An escape virus erupted onto the scene like a flash fire! Scientists found that “Subclade K” is a strain of influenza A (H3N2) that binds better to the membranes in our noses and is less sensitive to some antibodies (stuff that Infectious Diseases doctors love to chat about).1 Improved viral fitness means that chances are good that this escape virus will keep coming back until it is knocked off by a more fit flu strain. A big question last year was, “How effective are influenza vaccines going to be against the escape virus?” Thankfully, vaccine protection against hospitalization was pretty good, even among adults. But something extraordinary happened in kids who took the vaccine. While the vaccine protected adults against mild, moderate and severe flu only 32-39% of the time, kids were protected 70-79% of the time. It seems that children get more “bang for the buck” from influenza vaccine than adults. Also, for those who were not exposed to flu last year, this year’s influenza vaccines provide better protection against the escape virus. My coach made sure we got our flu shots because he didn’t want us watching from the sidelines. Years later, the science supports that same advice. Children receive remarkable protection from influenza vaccination, helping them avoid serious illness, stay out of the hospital and remain where they belong: in school, with their friends and families, and in the game. 1Al-Natour, L.M. 16 June 2026. Emerging Influenza A (H3N2) Subclade K: A narrative review. Natural Resources for Human Health, 6(3s). Pages 678-687. https://nrfhh.com/index.php/journal/article/view/522

supplementary_news.content_title: Get ready for flu season: Florida pharmacies rolling out new mRNA vaccines and updated COVID shots
supplementary_news.content: Florida pharmacies and clinics are now offering updated flu and COVID vaccines for the 2026-27 respiratory illness season, though some may be harder to find. Floridians can expect to find the new Moderna mRNA flu shot, mFLUSIVA, at some of their local pharmacies in the next few weeks, but not all. “It started shipping out over the weekend (following FDA release of lots), so it should be available in stores imminently,” said Christopher Ridley, a Moderna spokesman. The new vaccine’s mRNA technology , the same platform as Moderna’s COVID shots, provides about 27% more coverage against influenza than traditional flu vaccines, according to a study of 40,000 adults ages 50-64. The technology allows it to be updated more quickly to match circulating virus strains. An mRNA vaccine is one that is lab-produced that teaches your body how to fight off an illness versus a standard vaccine, which is made by using a weakened live version of a virus. However, because Moderna missed the early contracting cycle for the standard U.S. flu vaccine rollout, you may have to hunt for it. Moderna said shipping to major pharmacies will scale up progressively throughout the fall. Moderna has created a Vaccine Finder to locate its flu and COVID vaccines by ZIP code. Most major pharmacies in Florida have not committed to carry Moderna’s mFLUSIVA this respiratory illness season. “We’ll continue to evaluate Moderna’s new vaccine, as we do with all our offerings, to ensure we continue to meet the needs of the communities we serve,” said CVS spokeswoman Roslyn Guarino. ” We are not offering the mRNA flu vaccine currently.” Publix spokeswoman Lindsey Willis said: “The mRNA flu vaccine is not yet available. Our Publix Pharmacy offers the standard vaccine, as well as one of the preferentially recommended vaccines for ages 65+.” Robin Edie, a Walmart spokesperson, said: “We do not currently offer the mFLUVISA vaccine, but customers can speak with their local Walmart pharmacist about recommended vaccinations.” Walmart pharmacies are giving out the traditional flu shots. Walgreens likely will be the first in Florida to offer mFLUSIVA. “Walgreens will offer the new mRNA flu vaccine in limited quantities this season. Availability will vary by location. Patients interested in receiving the vaccine are encouraged to speak with their local Walgreens pharmacist for more information,” a spokesperson said. The new mFLUSIVA vaccine is not made with eggs, giving people with egg allergies another option. Side effects reported during the trials included arm soreness, headache, chills, and temporary fatigue. Those occurred slightly more frequently with mFLUSIVA than with traditional flu shots. Traditional flu shots Medical groups are urging Americans to get vaccinated for the flu after two difficult respiratory seasons. Last year, the dominant strain differed from previous years, so Americans had less natural defense against it. “We did have a really, really stressful and tough flu season last year,” said Julie Caldwell, Walgreens senior manager of immunizations. “You can’t predict what’s going to happen from season to season, so the best advice is to get protected.” Experts agree that almost everyone starting at age 6 months benefits from a flu vaccine. However, flu is particularly concerning for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems. During the 2024-2025 flu season, about 45,000 people in the United States lost their lives. The seasonal influenza vaccines don’t block all flu infections, but they do help prevent hospitalizations, especially for those most at risk, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project , a public health group based at the University of Minnesota. On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to see a doctor by 30% to 60%, according to U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. This year’s traditional flu shots cover three seasonal flu strains, and five manufacturers offer them. If you are shot-averse, you can choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if you’re ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria. The CDC recommends three preferred types of high-dose shots for adults 65 and older: Fluad (Adjuvanted), Fluzone High-Dose, or Flublok (Recombinant). Studies show all three high-dose shots perform significantly better than standard-dose flu vaccines at preventing hospitalization and severe illness in older adults. The mRNA flu vaccine hasn’t been fully studied in the 65+ group. However, it was granted accelerated approval for that age group after producing a stronger immune response than traditional vaccines, with similar rates of severe side effects. Moderna is conducting more studies to see how it stacks up against existing high-dose vaccines for adults in that age range. Walgreens’ Caldwell says her pharmacies, for now, will recommend the higher dose of the traditional flu vaccine for customers 65 and older. “That’s the CDC recommendation as well for patients 65 plus,” she said. Dr. T’Anjuihsien Marx, MDNow’s regional medical director for North Broward and Palm Beach County, said his clinics already have begun giving flu shots to patients. “For now, we are sticking with traditional flu shots, the tried and true,” he said. When to get the flu shot Experts say late September or October are the best times to get vaccinated for influenza, which typically starts spreading in November. Flu vaccines typically take a few weeks to reach full protection. Marx said he prefers late mid- to late-October. “It’s a guessing game when the flu season is going to hit, but I feel like October gives a better chance to take you through the whole season, especially if we get a late surge in February or March,” he said. Youngvet via Getty Images Experts say late September or October are the best times to get vaccinated for influenza, which typically starts spreading in November. Flu vaccines typically take a few weeks to reach full protection. What to know about this year’s COVID shots This year, the FDA has formally approved COVID vaccines for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older, or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk. However, medical groups recommend them for people 19 or older and say those 65 or older should get a second dose after six months. The fall COVID-19 vaccines have an updated formula targeting XFG, the dominant circulating strain. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children. Depending on age, people can choose a COVID shot and seek a pharmacy that offers it. Four types of shots have been approved: Pfizer’s COMIRNATY COVID-19 vaccine for those 5 years and older. Moderna’s SPIKEVAX for those 6 months and older. Moderna’s mNEXSPIKE, a lower-dose Moderna shot approved for ages 12 and older. Novavax’s NUVAXOVID, a non-mRNA vaccine, for those 12 years and older. Not all pharmacies and clinics will carry the Novavax vaccine but the company does have a vaccine locator . Caldwell said Walgreens will offer all types, but the Novavax shot will be available only at certain locations. “People can go into our scheduler and select what they want or say no preference,” she said. Should you get an RSV vaccine? RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, typically is a cold-like nuisance during the fall, winter and early spring. But it can be severe, even life-threatening, for infants and older adults. RSV caused an estimated 2.8 million to 5.8 million outpatient visits, between 170,000 and 340,000 hospitalizations and as many as 25,000 deaths last year in the United States, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project. The American Academy of Family Physicians recommends a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems. This season, there are three RSV vaccines: GSK, Pfizer, and Moderna. Caldwell said if you haven’t received the RSV vaccine, it’s just one dose, so consider getting that along with your COVID and flu shot in one visit. Cost and incentives Medicare covers the fall shots and most private health insurers say they plan to continue doing so through 2027. Most pharmacies take appointments or walk-ins. As an added benefit, several retailers are offering coupons with vaccinations. Patients who get a vaccine at Walgreens can earn $15 in Walgreens Cash rewards on their next in-store purchase of $5 or more as a myWalgreens® member. CVS offers a $5-off-$20 coupon after vaccination and Publix offers a $5 digital gift card after you receive your free flu shot. Walmart does not offer gift cards, cash bonuses, or rewards points for getting immunizations. South Florida Sun Sentinel health reporter Cindy Goodman can be reached at cgoodman@sunsentinel.com
